slides.title: Manipulation — what's hard
slides.body:
Robotic manipulation: making the robot do useful things WITH its hand. Sounds simple; isn't.

**Why it's hard**:

- **Forward + inverse kinematics**: from joint angles to end-effector pose, and back. Inverse kinematics has multiple solutions, singularities, and non-convexity.
- **Contact dynamics**: when the hand touches an object, friction, contact normals, slip — all matter. Hard to model + simulate.
- **Grasping**: predicting which grasp will succeed requires understanding object shape, mass, friction, and finger biomechanics.
- **Dexterous manipulation**: in-hand manipulation (rotating an object, writing with a pen) requires precise force + position control.

**Why it's a frontier**: humans do this trivially; robots have struggled for 50+ years. Recent ML approaches (RT-2, OpenVLA, π-0, diffusion policies) are the first to handle unstructured manipulation in real settings.

slides.title: Forward kinematics (FK)
slides.body:
**Forward kinematics**: given joint angles `q = [q_1, q_2, ..., q_n]`, compute the end-effector pose `T(q)`.

Use a kinematic chain: each joint contributes a transformation; chain them via matrix multiplication.

`T(q) = T_1(q_1) · T_2(q_2) · ... · T_n(q_n)`

Each `T_i` is a 4×4 homogeneous transformation matrix.

**Denavit-Hartenberg parameters**: a standardized way to assign coordinate frames to each link, simplifying the math. Every kinematics textbook has the conventions.

**FK is fast + unique**: given `q`, the end-effector pose is uniquely determined.

**Tooling**: `pinocchio` (C++/Python), KDL, MoveIt all implement FK. URDF (Unified Robot Description Format) is the standard way to specify the robot's geometry.

slides.title: Inverse kinematics (IK)
slides.body:
**Inverse kinematics**: given a desired end-effector pose `T_target`, find joint angles `q` such that `FK(q) = T_target`.

**Why it's harder**:

- **Multiple solutions**: a 7-DOF arm typically has infinitely many `q` for a given pose. Pick which one?
- **Singularities**: at certain `q`, the robot loses a degree of freedom (Jacobian rank drops). Velocities blow up.
- **No closed-form for most arms**: 6-DOF arms with specific geometry (Pieper arms) have closed-form. 7-DOF arms need iterative methods.
- **Joint limits**: not every `q` is feasible.

**Methods**:

- **Closed-form** (when geometry permits): analytic solution.
- **Newton-Raphson on the kinematic equations**: iterative; fast when initial guess is good.
- **Damped least squares (DLS)**: regularized version that handles singularities.
- **Optimization-based** (TRAC-IK, KDL-IK): minimize `||FK(q) - T_target||²` subject to joint limits.

IK is solved at every control step in production; computation budget is microseconds. Caching last solution as initial guess is essential.

question.question: Why does a 7-DOF robot arm typically have infinitely many IK solutions for a given end-effector pose?
options: It's redundant — 7 joints + 6 task-space dimensions = 1 redundant DOF. The 'elbow swivel' can be anywhere in a circle without affecting the end-effector pose. The redundancy is useful (for avoiding obstacles + singularities) but means IK isn't unique. Solving must include a way to pick one solution
question.explanation: 7-DOF arms are popular precisely because of redundancy. 6-DOF is the minimum to reach any pose; 7-DOF gives you a 1-D 'null space' to use for secondary objectives (avoiding obstacles, staying away from joint limits, energy minimization). The cost: IK must specify how to use the redundancy.

slides.title: Grasping
slides.body:
**Grasp planning**: where + how to grip an object so that picking it up succeeds.

**Classical methods**:

- **Form-closure**: contact points that fully constrain the object geometrically. Strong but rare.
- **Force-closure**: contact points + friction can resist any external wrench. The standard for parallel-jaw grippers.
- **Sampling-based**: sample candidate grasps; score by force-closure + reachability + clearance.

**ML-based grasping**:

- **Dex-Net**: train CNN to predict grasp success from depth images. Worked on cluttered scenes.
- **6-DoF GraspNet**: dense grasp prediction in 3D. Better generalization than 4-DoF planar grasping.
- **Diffusion-based grasping**: model the distribution of successful grasps; sample from it.

**Modern reality**: vision-based ML grasp prediction works well on novel objects in cluttered scenes. Used at Amazon (Sparrow), Boston Dynamics (Stretch), warehouse-automation startups.

**Open challenges**:

- Dexterous (multi-finger) grasping: harder optimization; less data; few production systems.
- Soft / deformable objects: contact models break down.
- High-precision assembly: requires force feedback + millimeter-precision control.

slides.title: Dexterous + contact-rich manipulation
slides.body:
Beyond pick-and-place, harder tasks:

- **Insertion** (peg-in-hole, USB plugs): millimeter precision; force feedback essential.
- **In-hand manipulation**: rotating, sliding, regrasping. Requires multi-finger dexterity.
- **Tool use**: using a hammer, screwdriver, pen.
- **Bimanual + multi-arm**: two arms cooperating.

**Why these are hard**:

- **Contact dynamics**: highly nonlinear; hard to simulate accurately.
- **Friction uncertainty**: same finger on the same object slips differently every time.
- **Visual occlusion**: the hand occludes its own contacts; vision feedback insufficient.

**Modern approaches**:

- **Sim-to-real with domain randomization**: train in simulation; randomize physics + visuals; transfer to real.
- **Hierarchical RL**: learn high-level policy in simulation; low-level controller from human demonstrations.
- **Tactile sensing**: GelSight, DIGIT-style high-resolution tactile sensors give the robot 'fingertips'.
- **Diffusion policies**: model the distribution over action sequences; sample policies that handle contact uncertainty.

**Production status**:

- Pick-and-place: solved for many cases.
- Insertion: solved for known geometries with force feedback; harder for novel objects.
- General dexterous manipulation: research frontier. RT-2, π-0, Tesla Optimus all aimed here.

question.question: Why is contact-rich manipulation (insertion, dexterous tasks) harder than pick-and-place?
options: Contact dynamics are highly nonlinear and hard to model + simulate. Friction is uncertain; small position errors cause large force changes; vision is occluded by the hand. Pick-and-place mostly avoids continuous contact (open-grip → close → lift), so the hard contact problem is brief. Insertion + dexterous tasks live in continuous contact
question.explanation: Continuous contact is the central difficulty. Friction, contact normals, slip, deformation all matter and all are hard to model. Sim-to-real for contact-rich tasks requires more careful domain randomization and often tactile feedback. This is why production manipulators do pick-and-place well + dexterous tasks poorly.

slides.title: The path forward
slides.body:
Manipulation has been the slowest-progressing area of robotics for decades. The recent shift:

**Old paradigm** (2010s): hand-engineered controllers + carefully-engineered tasks. Brittle; doesn't transfer.

**New paradigm** (2020s): learn end-to-end policies from demonstrations + RL. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models like RT-2, OpenVLA, π-0 trained on diverse robot data. Transfer across objects, tasks, embodiments — to a degree.

**Open frontiers**:

- **Generalization across embodiments**: a policy trained on one robot working on a different robot.
- **Long-horizon tasks**: a policy that plans + executes 10+ subtasks.
- **Few-shot adaptation**: novel object + novel task, learned from a single demonstration.
- **Tactile-vision-language fusion**: integrating tactile feedback with vision + language commands.
- **Common-sense physical reasoning**: knowing that pushing one block knocks over its neighbor.

The next lesson covers learning-based control more broadly. The frontier lesson at the end of the path covers the foundation-models-for-robotics era explicitly.

slides.title: Why IK is harder than FK
slides.body:
**Forward kinematics (FK)**: given joint angles $\theta$, compute end-effector pose $T = f(\theta)$. Always solvable; just composition of joint transformations.

**Inverse kinematics (IK)**: given desired end-effector pose $T$, find joint angles $\theta = f^{-1}(T)$. Hard for several reasons:

1. **Multiple solutions**: a 6-DOF arm typically has up to 16 distinct IK solutions for a generic pose. Which one to use? Depends on joint-limit feasibility, current configuration (smallest motion from where we are), singularities to avoid.
2. **Redundancy**: a 7-DOF arm has a 1-DOF nullspace — infinitely many IK solutions. Free dimension can be used for secondary tasks (avoid obstacles, stay away from joint limits).
3. **Singularities**: configurations where the Jacobian loses rank. The arm is mechanically valid but the local linearization is degenerate — moving the end-effector in one direction requires infinite joint velocities. Standard robot configurations (e.g., elbow fully extended) are singular.

**Solving IK**: closed-form for simple geometries (Pieper's solution for 6-DOF with three concurrent axes); numerical (Jacobian-pseudoinverse, damped least-squares) for the general case; learned (DNN-based IK) for problems with constraints that defy closed form.

**Force control**: instead of commanding joint angles, command end-effector forces. Used for assembly tasks (insertion, polishing) where contact dynamics matter. Hybrid position/force control (Khatib): position-control in some directions, force-control in others — the standard for sensitive assembly.

question.question: A 6-DOF robot arm at a near-singular configuration:
options: Has fewer IK solutions than usual.
Has high joint velocities required to move the end-effector — small motions become numerically unstable.
Has more IK solutions than usual.
question.explanation: Near a singularity, the Jacobian becomes ill-conditioned. Small end-effector motions require large joint velocities; the system is hard to control reliably. Standard mitigation: damped least-squares IK (Levenberg-Marquardt-style damping) handles near-singular Jacobian gracefully but at the cost of less-direct tracking near the singularity. Path planners avoid singularities entirely.

hints: What's special about the Jacobian at a singularity?
If small Cartesian motions require huge joint motions, what does that imply for control?
slides.workedSolution: Near a singularity the Jacobian $J(\theta)$ has a small singular value. $\theta' = J^+(\theta) v$ for end-effector velocity $v$ — small singular values of $J$ become large in $J^+$, so $\theta'$ explodes for finite $v$. In practice the arm's motion becomes jerky / unstable, and the control system can saturate joint velocities. Damped least-squares IK regularizes by adding $\lambda I$ to $J^T J$, sacrificing tracking accuracy for stability.
